summaries.headline: Report Links Career Literacy to Job Security
summaries.summary: A new report from The DeBruce Foundation finds that career literacy — the ability to understand, plan, and navigate career pathways over a lifetime — strongly predicts employment security in today's volatile job market. Drawing on nationally representative surveys of roughly 36,000 Americans ages 18-64 conducted between 2021 and 2025, the report ties career literacy to higher incomes, greater satisfaction with nonwage benefits, stronger long-term savings, and better ability to weather job disruptions and transitions. As labor markets grow less predictable, the findings put fresh weight behind K-12 career readiness efforts that go beyond exposure to a single pathway and instead build students' capacity to navigate shifting career terrain over decades.

summaries.headline: Colorado Districts Lose Transgender Athlete Lawsuit
summaries.summary: A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit from eight Colorado districts and charter schools—including District 49, Colorado Springs District 11, and Academy District 20—challenging the state's non-discrimination protections for transgender students, ruling the plaintiffs lack standing because they face no clear harm. The decision, issued by Senior U.S. District Court Judge John Kane, upholds a January magistrate ruling and comes after the Colorado High School Activities Association separately settled with the districts in December, agreeing not to penalize schools with policies barring transgender athletes from teams matching their gender identity. With the state not currently enforcing penalties against districts that maintain such policies, the ruling leaves the underlying tension between local school board policies and state law unresolved rather than settled.

summaries.headline: Newark Cuts Chronic Absenteeism to Record Low
summaries.summary: Newark Public Schools' chronic absenteeism rate fell to 8.5% for the 2025-26 school year, the lowest mark in district history and well below the state's most recent rate of 14.4%. The district has cut chronic absenteeism from a high of 29.7% in 2016-17 and 27% in 2018-19, with Black students and students with disabilities posting the largest gains this year, according to district data presented at Thursday's board meeting. The turnaround comes after years in which Newark risked a state-imposed corrective action plan over attendance, underscoring how sustained, targeted intervention can move a metric that's proven stubborn in many large urban districts.

summaries.headline: Nursery Rhymes Fade, Taking Literacy Groundwork With Them
summaries.summary: Early childhood experts warn that nursery rhymes, once a staple of family downtime and early education, are disappearing from both homes and classrooms, even as kindergarten readiness checklists still expect children to recognize sounds, letters, and rhymes. W. Steven Barnett, director of the National Institute for Early Education Research, calls rhymes "almost brilliant in their simplicity" for building phonological awareness without any specialized training or materials, yet anecdotal evidence suggests they've largely vanished from preschool and kindergarten curricula. As districts search for cost-effective ways to close early literacy gaps, the quiet disappearance of a free, low-tech tool raises questions about what else has been lost in the shift toward more formalized instruction.

summaries.headline: Ohio's "State Share" Funding Statistic Draws Scrutiny
summaries.summary: Ohio district officials have circulated a claim that the state's share of K-12 funding has fallen to a historic low of 32 percent, fueling narratives of state "disinvestment" in public schools even as per-pupil spending has climbed 17 percent since 2013 to an average of $16,976. Fordham Institute analysis counters that the 32 percent figure reflects an internal funding-formula mechanism, not actual state contributions, and that the true state share sits closer to 44 percent once all state funds and the mandatory 20-mill local property tax floor are factored in. For district leaders and policymakers navigating funding debates, the dispute underscores how technical formula details can distort public understanding of who's actually paying for schools.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Delays Extra Funding for Arts School
summaries.summary: The Chicago school board postponed for a second time a vote on steering an additional $5.5 million to Chicago Arts High School, on top of $5.7 million already budgeted for its transition into a district-run campus. Board supporters argue the extra funds are needed to preserve the school's conservatory model, which pairs academics with training from roughly 70 professional teaching artists, but district officials warn the money would have to come from the budgets of 72 other arts schools across the system. The delay, pushed to a Sept. 10 vote, underscores the tension facing districts trying to honor commitments to save individual schools while managing deficits that leave little room for exceptions.

summaries.headline: Indianapolis Schools Bring Back Zeros, With Conditions
summaries.summary: Indianapolis Public Schools reversed its six-year-old no-zero grading policy, voting unanimously to let students in grades 1-12 receive a zero on assignments they make no attempt to complete after multiple opportunities and teacher support. Under the previous policy, the lowest possible score was 50%; now students who make a good-faith effort will still earn at least 50%, while those who don't engage at all can fail outright, with grade bands set roughly 10 points apart. The reversal, driven largely by teacher feedback that the old system was hard to implement and didn't prepare students for college, signals a broader recalibration of pandemic-era grading policies as districts weigh accountability against second chances.

summaries.headline: Custer Exits Chicago School Board President Race
summaries.summary: Jennifer Custer, an incumbent Chicago Board of Education member, withdrew from the race to become the district's first elected board president, citing an unwillingness to compete against special interests prepared to spend millions on the contest. Custer was the only candidate in the field whose petition signatures went unchallenged, and her exit leaves four contenders: incumbent Jessica Biggs, former CTU political director Hilario Dominguez, attorney Victor Henderson, and consultant Sendhil Revuluri. Custer built a reputation for independence since narrowly winning her seat in 2024 with CTU backing, recently casting the lone dissenting vote against mayoral-allied referendums on raising CPS revenue, and her departure from the race narrows the field just as questions loom over who will set the tone for the district's newly elected governance structure.

summaries.headline: Denver Superintendent's School Tour Masks Deeper Tensions
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools Superintendent Alex Marrero kicked off the 2026-27 school year with a first-day tour of five southwest Denver schools, joining Mayor Mike Johnston on the playground swings at Goldrick Elementary before heading to classrooms at CMS Community School, Rocky Mountain Prep Westwood, DSST College View, and Denison Montessori. The lighthearted visit comes as Colorado's largest district navigates a bell-to-bell cellphone ban, potential school closures, two federal fights with the Trump administration, and a $44 million mill levy override on the November ballot — all against a backdrop of reported friction between Marrero and the school board that hires and fires him. Only two of seven board members joined the tour, a small but telling detail suggesting the superintendent's public goodwill push is running parallel to, not in sync with, his governance challenges at home.

summaries.headline: NYC's AI Policy Delay Freezes School Software Buys
summaries.summary: New York City principals are heading toward a Sept. 10 first day of school without clarity on whether they can access electronic gradebooks and family communication platforms, casualties of a purchasing freeze Chancellor Kamar Samuels imposed in early July while the district reworks its AI guidance. The freeze has blocked routine software renewals, including tools with no AI component that schools have used for years, with four administrators telling Chalkbeat they still don't know what's allowed just weeks before students arrive. The delay traces back to an initial AI policy released in March that drew fierce backlash from parents and that Samuels himself later admitted "missed the mark," leaving districts to absorb the operational fallout while the Education Department offers no timeline for resolution.

summaries.headline: Public Schools Eye New Federal Tax Credit Cash
summaries.summary: A federal tax credit program created under Trump's tax overhaul, originally designed to help families pay for private school and homeschool costs, includes a provision that lets public schools tap the same funding stream. Treasury guidance released in June allows specific nonprofits to collect donations that taxpayers direct from their federal returns toward public school expenses like transportation and tutoring, opening a path for district foundations to court donors much like private school voucher programs already do. As districts like Denver Public Schools begin exploring this avenue, the shift signals a new, more formalized fundraising infrastructure for public education — one that mirrors the mechanisms critics once feared would exclusively favor private alternatives.

summaries.headline: Students Skip the AI Tutor They're Given
summaries.summary: A new study of Khanmigo, the AI chatbot built into Khan Academy, found that middle schoolers in a Tennessee district rarely used it even when access was universal, engaging with the tool only about a third of the days they worked in the program. Researchers, who randomly assigned low-performing students across 18 middle schools to use Khan Academy versus other digital math tools plus teacher-led small groups, found the Khan group did post faster math gains by year two — but attributed that progress to the platform's structure, not the AI, since many interactions with Khanmigo amounted to off-topic chatter or attempts to extract answers outright. The findings echo Sal Khan's own assessment that the tutor is a "non-event" for most students, suggesting that personalized-learning gains may still hinge on human attention rather than the AI layer districts are increasingly paying for.

summaries.headline: Wisconsin Governor's Race Puts School Funding in Play
summaries.summary: Wisconsin's open governor's race arrives as outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, a former state superintendent, leaves behind a legacy of education as a top state policy priority. WUWM's Katherine Kokal spoke with WisPolitics.com political editor JR Ross to unpack how the race could reshape approaches to school funding and voucher programs heading into the midterms. With Evers exiting, district leaders and advocates on both sides of the voucher debate are watching closely to see whether his successor maintains, expands, or scales back the state's education funding priorities.

summaries.headline: Minnesota Voters to Decide School Trust Fund Payout
summaries.summary: Minnesota voters will decide on Nov. 3 whether to amend the state constitution to update how funds are distributed from the Permanent School Fund, a trust established in 1858 to support public, charter and tribal schools. The fund has grown from roughly $675 million in 2010 to more than $2.3 billion today, but the current distribution formula hasn't kept pace, and the change would add up to $40 more per student if approved. Superintendent Jim Wagner cautioned that an unanswered question counts as a "no" vote and warned the item's placement on the back of the ballot could cause it to be overlooked, even as he noted passage alone won't resolve his district's broader financial pressures.

summaries.headline: Mamdani Scraps $200M School Internet Contract
summaries.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is canceling the T-Mobile internet service tied to a $330 million Adams-era contract that equipped 350,000 student Chromebooks with free connectivity, citing unnecessary overlap with existing services and a citywide push to close a multibillion-dollar budget gap. The internet portion alone cost the city roughly $3.5 million per month, and officials say students who still need service can get it through an existing Verizon-based program for $10 per student per month, a fraction of the prior cost. The cut lands as districts nationally face pressure to justify large-scale ed-tech spending amid tightening budgets and growing scrutiny over whether device-heavy strategies actually translate into better student outcomes.

summaries.headline: Curriculum Arrives as AI Guidance Lags Behind Use
summaries.summary: Common Sense Media has completed its free K-12 Digital Literacy & Well-Being Curriculum with a new high school program covering AI literacy, online harms and digital well-being, timed to new research showing 70% of U.S. teens already use AI for schoolwork. Only 27% of surveyed teens said a teacher had ever discussed what AI is and how it works, and fewer than a third had covered safe use or how to judge AI-generated accuracy, even as students describe nuanced habits like rewriting answers in their own voice or using AI to check completed work. Nearly 40% of teen AI users say they're missing out on learning or generating fewer original ideas because of it, leaving districts to close an instructional gap that student behavior has already outpaced.

summaries.headline: DOE Guidance Turns Edtech Evidence Into Procurement Rule
summaries.summary: The U.S. Department of Education released a Dear Colleague letter on Aug. 20 that reframes edtech adoption from an engagement metric to a performance requirement, pushing districts to justify purchases with outcomes data rather than usage stats like log-ins. The letter adds no new federal regulations, but it supplies language on measurable student outcomes and implementation proof that procurement directors, CIOs, and curriculum leaders can expect to see embedded in RFPs, evaluation checkpoints, and contract terms. For vendors and district leaders alike, the practical effect lands well before any rulemaking would: the next bid cycle, not federal enforcement, is where this guidance will actually bite.

summaries.headline: Fiscal Red Flags Are Nearly Universal in Big Districts
summaries.summary: A Reason Foundation analysis of the nation's 100 largest school districts found only two operating without any fiscal warning signs, with districts averaging 2.4 out of 8 tracked risk indicators. That performance is worse than any other level of government examined, pointing to widespread structural budget pressures rather than isolated mismanagement. As enrollment shifts, pandemic aid runoff, and rising costs converge, district finance chiefs and school boards face a tightening margin for error heading into budget season.

summaries.headline: Column Defends Education's Professional Organizations
summaries.summary: A guest columnist in The Virginian-Pilot argues that recent attacks on professional education organizations amount to attacks on public education itself, even when critics don't frame them that way. The piece traces the lineage of professional associations back to the Massachusetts Historical Society in 1791 and the standard-setting bodies born during the Industrial Revolution, noting how groups like the American Medical Association and American Bar Association shaped licensure, ethics and public trust in their fields. The argument lands on education associations today providing the same function—research-backed best practices, peer networks and leadership development—suggesting that weakening these institutions strips away the infrastructure that keeps educators current and accountable.

summaries.headline: A Superintendent's Literacy Struggle Shapes District Strategy
summaries.summary: Providence Public Schools Superintendent Javier Montañez, who struggled to read as a child, now spends time in kindergarten classrooms modeling phonics lessons alongside teachers as part of the district's push on early literacy. The visit to Robert Bailey Elementary's summer learning program shows a leader treating foundational reading skills as personal mission rather than abstract policy goal, down to sounding out letters and cheering on 5-year-olds during attendance songs. Providence's approach — pairing lived experience with hands-on presence in classrooms — offers a model for how district leaders can signal that early literacy is a top-level priority, not just a program buried in a curriculum office.

CHARLOTTE — [Crisis Assistance Ministry](https://crisisassistance.org/ "https://crisisassistance.org/") and Bank of America are partnering to help Union and Anson County families save more money.

Bank of America advisers visit Crisis Assistance Ministry once a month to provide financial literacy education through a new program called “Better Money Habits.”

“The goal for them is to just feel relieved, lift their troubles and feel confident in financial decisions,” said Heather Gardner, executive director of Crisis Assistance Ministry.

There are 12 men in the program now with plans to expand.

Crisis Assistance Ministry also helps families cover utility bills and avoid eviction.

# Dolly Parton’s Children’s Literacy Legacy

By Shannon Maughan

\|



Aug 27, 2026


![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

Audio Native

Listen to This Article

00:00

12:00

1.0x

[\|\|ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io/?utm_medium=audionative&utm_source=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.publishersweekly.com%2Fpw%2Fby-topic%2Fchildrens%2Fchildrens-industry-news%2Farticle%2F101140-dolly-parton-s-children-s-literacy-legacy.html&utm_campaign=audionative_www.publishersweekly.com&utm_term=creator_public_id_81a124bca97e51d9f8d64cf4076617209c536192d26bc409a4172a6d3defc042&utm_content=project_id_1dlJuRhJXGvTQVCkijy5)

![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

Beloved entertainment icon Dolly Parton, who died at age 80 on August 25 after facing cancer, was a woman of many talents—country music superstar, entrepreneur, and philanthropist among them. But she took particular pride in her role as a fierce children’s literacy advocate and founder of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, a program that gifts enrolled children one book per month from birth to age five. The program recently celebrated its 31st year and to date has given away more than 330 million books to more than three million registered children across the U.S., Canada, U.K., Republic of Ireland, and Australia. This week Parton’s death has sparked renewed awareness of Imagination Library and reinvigorated donations. Kids, families, and champions of children’s literacy everywhere hope that these developments will help keep Parton’s legacy alive in a climate of legislative budget cuts and household belt tightening.

Through her Dollywood Foundation, Parton created the Imagination Library in 1995 as a tribute to her father, who felt shame over his inability to read or write, something she believed prevented him from realizing his dreams. “Inspiring kids to love to read became my passion and my mission,” she said in a welcome video on [the program’s website](https://imaginationlibrary.com/), noting that books often inspire children’s dreams for their future, and “if you can read you can teach yourself anything.”

Initially, the Imagination Library was designed to serve children in Sevier County in East Tennessee, where Parton grew up. The idea of mailing a child a book each month ensures a level of excitement and engagement and is supported by a body of research that shows having books at home is one of the strongest predictors of children’s academic success, regardless of income or their parents’ education. By 2000, the program had experienced solid success, and a [nationwide expansion](https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/by-topic/childrens/childrens-book-news/article/92981-dolly-parton-s-imagination-library-expands-national-reach.html) of the concept was underway. Tennessee was the first to take Imagination Library statewide in 2004, and there are now more than 15 states that have done the same. The program expanded [beyond U.S. borders](https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/newsbrief/index.html?record=5490) as well.

In the Imagination Library program framework, the Dollywood Foundation covers overhead and administrative costs and coordinates the selection and purchase of books, while teaming up with local 501(c)(3) program partners who promote the program, enroll young readers in their community, and pay $2.60 per child each month towards mailing and book expenses. The United Way adopted Imagination library as one of its strategies to increase childhood literacy early on, and globally, United Ways remain Imagination Library’s most frequent partner.

![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

On the book side, Penguin Young Readers became the official publisher for the Imagination Library in 2001, “in response to the immense interest in the literacy program from all areas of the country and the need to provide a wider breadth of classic, beloved, and contemporary children’s board and picture books for the program,” according to PYR president Jen Loja.

In 2017, several years after the Penguin Group and Random House merger was finalized in 2013, the Imagination Library grew to include Random House Children’s Books titles. And in 2024, DK titles were added to the mix “when a fully bilingual—English/Spanish—version of the Imagination Library made its debut,” Loja said.

“The very first order processed was for 3,600 copies of six different titles,” she recalled. “This number has risen exponentially over the decades as we strive to meet the needs of Imagination Library’s meteoric growth while always preserving Dolly’s singular mission— ‘that you can never get enough books into the hands of enough children.’ ”

In the U.S., a Blue Ribbon Selection Committee consisting of early childhood literacy experts crafts the lists of age-appropriate titles from PRH for the program each year. But a couple of books have become mainstays: the first title sent to every child who signs up for the Imagination Library is an edition of _The Little Engine That Could_ by Watty Piper, illustrated by Dan Santat and containing an introduction by Parton; and the month that an enrolled child turns five, they receive a copy of _Look Out Kindergarten, Here I Come!_ by Nancy Carlson.

“One of the things we are proudest of in our work with Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is its reach,” Loja said. “We hear again and again about a child’s joy when a book arrives in their mailbox, and the pride of owning their own books. They are amazed and delighted to see their names on the address label affixed to each copy. This sets them on the path of being a lifelong reader and it’s what sets the Dolly Parton Imagination Library apart.”

Lisa Vitelli, VP and director, premium literacy sales at PRH, said: “For more than 26 years, it has been one of the great privileges of our professional lives to be part of this remarkable effort. Our teams are heartbroken by the loss of Dolly Parton, and deeply grateful to have played a role in one of her most cherished and lasting gifts to the world. We will continue that work with the utmost pride and care, just as we know she would have wanted.”

Maria A. Pallante, president and CEO, Association of American Publishers, whose organization presented Parton with one of its first AAP Honors Awards in 2020 in recognition of her Imagination Library efforts, said: “Dolly Parton lived a magnificent life focused on creativity, compassion, and joy. In addition to her inspiring personal journey and singular reputation as a singer-songwriter, she was a widely read book author and reading advocate, dedicated to giving children their very own books to hold, read, and keep through her Imagination Library. Dolly was truly one of a kind and the publishing community will miss her tremendously.”

![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

**A chorus of support**

As people around the world mourn Parton, they have also been honoring her by committing to her Imagination Library mission. In Pennsylvania, literacy nonprofit Reading Ready Pittsburgh is one of three local partners bringing the library to the region. They began by offering the program in several zip codes just outside the city in the Mon Valley in 2020, and in 2024 were able to expand coverage and become the permanent host of Imagination Library for the city of Pittsburgh. In all, more than 9,000 kids are currently enrolled, and the number has begun to tick up since Parton’s death.

“The family of Dolly Parton has requested that in lieu of flowers they wanted donations to local Imagination Library programs,” said Mary Denison, Reading Ready Pittsburgh’s executive director. “We’ve been getting donations for the last 24 hours \[August 25–26\], well over $3,000 at this point. People have been very generous in her name. The other thing that’s happened in the last 24 hours is that we’ve had numerous people enroll their kids. I’m sure that would have pleased Dolly a lot.”

The Imagination Library of Washington enrolls nearly 85,000 children and has distributed roughly 4.5 million books since it began expansion work to become a statewide program in 2022, according to executive director Brooke Fisher-Clark. “It’s heartwarming to see how many people we have reached to this point,” she said. “The Imagination Library is beloved by everyone in our state, and everyone is heartbroken at the loss of Dolly. We’re committed more than ever to maintaining and sustaining this program for generations to come.”

But sustaining the program has become more challenging in recent months since Imagination Library Washington’s state funding was cut in the 2026 legislative session. As a result, some communities had to pause their service. “State funding to support the book match is critical for that public-private partnership, where 50% is the state and the other 50% is provided by local communities to support their local programs,” Fisher-Clark said. “It was disheartening that we were not included in that. But we were very grateful to have received a life ring of support from two generous foundations that were able to step in and provide some bridge assistance, so that we could continue to provide a match in the absence of the legislature and also help some of our struggling regions to support the local funding level.”

Fisher-Clark said that Imagination Library Washington, like many partners nationwide, has also seen increased interest in the program this week. “It’s really beautiful to see everyone rally together,” she said. “The outpouring of support in emails and calls that we received, in addition to some of the donations we’ve seen come through, is just amazing. And I think Dolly is smiling down right now and is really proud of seeing everyone come together for our kids.”

![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

**Dolly Parton: A partial bibliography**

Dolly Parton not only talked literacy, she walked it. She was an avid reader as well as an author in her own right. As a child, “I used to read everything I could get my hands on at school, I loved fairy tales” she told Terry Gross in a 2001 interview on NPR’s _Fresh Air_. “I still love books. I read everything—I read whatever the hit books are on the bestseller list, and people give me gifts.”

Parton made her children’s book debut in 1994 with _[My Coat of Many Colors](https://www.publishersweekly.com/9780060234133)_, illustrated by Judith Sutton (HarperCollins), and adapted from the lyrics of her song of the same name. More recently, she created a three-book series about a French bulldog, beginning with _[Billy the Kid Makes It Big](https://www.publishersweekly.com/9780593661574)_, illustrated by MacKenzie Haley (Penguin Workshop, 2023).

She’s also the subject of several books for young readers. _Dolly Parton: A Little Golden Book Biography_ by Deborah Hopkinson, illustrated by Monique Dong (Golden, 2021), has sold half a million copies to date. It’s the second bestselling title in the series, topped only by _Taylor Swift_. Others include _Who Is Dolly Parton?_ by True Kelley, illustrated by Stephen Marchesi (Penguin Workshop, 2014); and _I Am Dolly Parton_ by Brad Meltzer, illustrated by Christopher Eliopoulos (Rocky Pond, 2022).

Among her books for adults, she crafted three photographic memoirs beginning with 2020’s _Dolly Parton, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics_, written with Robert K. Oermann (Chronicle); and collaborated with James Patterson on the thriller _[Run, Rose, Run](https://www.publishersweekly.com/9780759554344)_ (Little, Brown, 2022), which featured a protagonist who was a Nashville musician.

# Dolly Parton's Imagination Library delivered 5.3 million books to foster early literacy in Mecklenburg Co. kids since 2014

Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has transformed lives in Mecklenburg County, delivering 5.3 million free books to children since 2014, fostering early literacy.

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Dolly Parton built a career around telling stories— but one of her most important stories may be the one she never had to sing.

“The Dolly Parton Imagination Library is, of course, focused on literacy, early literacy. This program came to Smart Start of Mecklenburg in 2014,” Smart Start Mecklenburg County CEO Mike Blackwelder said.

![](https://www.wcnc.com/assets/shared-images/icons/arrow-circle-down.svg)
This story continues below.


More in Education


- [Dolly Parton's Imagination Library lives on in Mecklenburg County after her death](https://www.wcnc.com/article/news/local/dolly-parton-imagination-library-mecklenburg-county-death/275-9141b8f7-16fd-4baf-8f01-723b09cb37ea)
- [Remembering Dolly Parton's lifetime of philanthropy](https://www.wcnc.com/video/life/remembering-dolly-partons-lifetime-of-philanthropy/275-1a2d07a0-54e3-4f8c-9748-c1d9d5f8bf41)
- [Charlotte Amateur Tennis Championships return for 8th year. Here's what you can expect](https://www.wcnc.com/video/entertainment/events/testing/275-e089160c-8a67-4d6c-b746-0f032efe6602)

The story of the Imagination Library began for her in her home in East Tennessee.

“Dolly, herself, started the program in Sevier County, Tennessee where she grew up. Her father was actually — he lived his entire life never knowing to read or write, and she saw what what difficulty that brought to him and what reading and education can do for a person, what doors it could open," Blackwelder said. "So, she wanted to give that gift to other people, and who knows if she ever knew it would be worldwide, but millions of books have been given out to her ever since — 5.3 million just in Mecklenburg County over the years.”

That’s the legacy Blackwelder says Dolly leaves behind here through the organization’s initiative of free, age-appropriate books in the hands of Mecklenburg County children.

“Ages zero to five, until their fifth birthday, and every month they get a new book in the mail and it gives them the chance to read with their families, promote early literacy and get them ready for kindergarten," he said.

Through Smart Start and Imagination Library, Mecklenburg County gives away about 375,000 books a year, and has distributed roughly 5.3 million since 2014.

Something longtime educator Lori Dalia says she fully supports, along with everything else Dolly represented.

“I’ve always admired her. I love Dollywood, and I really do appreciate all her philanthropy and her humanitarianism. I don’t think we have enough of those people around right now," Dalia said.

Smart Start says the best the best way to honor Dolly's legacy is to keep that mission going, getting books into the hands of children and helping families build a love of reading. For ways to sign up, visit [Smart Start](https://www.smartstartofmeck.org/).

# Arkansas Imagination Library says Dolly Parton’s gift of literacy ‘reached every county’ in state



August 26, 2026



by



El Dorado News-Times




Comments

[...](https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2026/aug/26/arkansas-imagination-library-says-dolly-partons/#insticator-commenting)

×![Books sent from the Dolly Parton Imagination Library to a home in Rogers are shown in this Feb. 13, 2014, file photo. (NWA Democrat-Gazette file photo)](https://wehco.media.clients.ellingtoncms.com/img/photos/2026/08/26/Imagination_003_crop_t320.jpg?fa67021387348b8667950d2a49bd5d6642c5ab68)

Let us read it for you. Listen now.
Your browser does not support the audio element.


EL DORADO -- While the late Dolly Parton called the neighboring state of Tennessee her home, her impact as the Book Lady is felt in all 75 Arkansas counties.

In a Facebook ode to the singer-songwriter, the Democratic Party of Arkansas called Parton "a trailblazer for literacy, for libraries (and) for medical research."

Parton's Imagination Library mails children one free book monthly until their fifth birthday. In a 2023 interview with Arkansas TV, she said she started the program in the 1990s to honor her father, who couldn't read or write.

"My dad was involved in it. He took such pride in hearing kids call me The Book Lady," Parton said. "Education is everything. ... If you can read, you can self-educate yourself."

Since 2005, the Arkansas-based program claims it has delivered more than 7 million books, and 140,000 5-year-olds have graduated from Imagination Library. Of the state's newborn to 5-year-olds, more than 82,000 are enrolled, the organization says online.

"Here in Arkansas, Dolly's vision has reached every county in our state," Arkansas Imagination Library said Tuesday on Facebook. "Thank you, Dolly, for believing so deeply in the power of books and the potential of every child. Your legacy will live on for generations. We will always love you."

U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., acknowledged the impact of the program on Natural State youth.

"Dolly Parton was an icon. Her music brought joy to generations," he said in a statement. "Through her Imagination Library, she gave books to thousands of Arkansas kids and helped them learn to love to read. Anna and I join Arkansans in mourning Dolly's death and celebrating her extraordinary life."

In Union County, enrollment for the program is administered through the United Way of Union County. The program serves hundreds of children throughout the county, including El Dorado, Calion, Norphlet, Smackover, Strong and Junction City, said Tyler Turner, executive director of the United Way.

The library and its reach in the county crystallize the legacies of Parton and a beloved member of the community who was instrumental in launching the local program in 2011.

Alexis Alexander, 50, died in 2023 due to an illness, 12 years after she worked to establish an Imagination Library in her roles as executive director of the United Way of Union County and a "big Dolly Parton fan."

"Just like anything, it started with a handful of registrations, and the good news is, it has grown," Turner said, reporting that for the first time in July, the program broke through 1,600 books to be mailed to Union County children in a single month.

The monthly average is 1,540 books, according to a 2025 report from the United Way.

In 2025, Imagination Library mailed 18,430 books to 1,947 children in Union County, with the heaviest concentration in El Dorado.

More than 200,000 books have been sent out to participants in the county since the inception of the program.

Turner explained that the mailings are coordinated by the Dollywood Foundation, but the United Way serves as a local champion of Imagination Library by keeping track of registrations and providing funding for local operations.

Turner said the cost to operate the program is approximately $31 per child, which comes to more than $51,000 each year in Union County.

United Way relies on savings, grants, fundraisers, endowments and a donation from Alexander's estate to make up half of the annual Imagination Library budget and partners with the Imagination Library of Arkansas, which covers the other half of the cost to enroll children in local programs around the state.

Turner emphasized that United Way does not use campaign funds that are raised each year for Imagination Library.

Campaign funds are distributed to United Way's partner agencies to support literacy, education and animal services and other causes

As more families enroll children earlier, kids are receiving more books because they remain in the program longer before aging out at 5, said Turner.

The welcoming book for Imagination Library is "The Little Engine That Could."

"That is a cool message for children," he said.
